list.listitem: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines recommend routinely obtaining a sexual history from patients and encouraging risk reduction by offering prevention counseling. C

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF, 2021) recommends screening for all women aged 24 years and younger and those who are older and at high risk for chlamydia or gonorrhea infections using a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT). B
Screening men does not have sufficient evidence, so the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) cannot recommend for or against this practice. C
The USPSTF (2020) recommends behavioral counseling for all sexually active adolescents and for adults who are at increased risk for STIs. B

For urogenital infections, optimal specimen types for gonorrhea screening using NAATs include first-void urine for men and vaginal swab specimens for women. A Patient-collected samples can be used in place of provider-collected samples in clinical settings when testing by NAAT. B

Treat gonococcal infection of the cervix, urethra, pharynx and/or rectum with ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly (IM). Patients weighing more than 300 pounds should be given a dose of 1 gram. If chlamydia infection has not been excluded, add doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days or if pregnant a single dose of azithromycin 1 gram orally.(Centers for Disease Control and Prevention).A
The STI 2021 guidelines recommend a test of cure at 7-14 days after initial treatment for anyone with pharyngeal gonorrhea using either culture or NAAT. B
Reinfection rates are high, so all with gonorrhea infections should be retested at 3 to 4 months. A
All individuals with the diagnosis of gonorrhea should be offered HIV testing. C

background.definition: Bacterial infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which is a Gram-negative diplococcus.

list.listitem: In 2023, according to the CDC, there were 601,319 cases of gonorrhea reported in the United States or 179.5 cases per 100,000 population. This represents a continued rate decrease from 2021. Rates of gonorrhea in 2023 were higher in men than women (228.3 cases per 100,000 males vs. 130.7 cases per 100,000 females). This represents a decrease for both, but greater for women since 2021.

Gonorrhea rates in 2023 were highest among Blacks (557.8 per 100,000 population) followed by American Indians/Alaskan Natives (292.2 cases per 100,000 population), Native Hawaiians/Other Pacific Islanders (181.3 cases per 100,000 population), Hispanics (128.8 cases per 100,000 population), and Whites (67.1 cases per 100,000 population).

In a 3-year population study of 1,293,423 US women of whom about 60% were tested during pregnancy, 3.5% (26,437 of 761,315) and 0.6% (4605 of 730,796) tested positive for chlamydial and gonococcal infection, respectively, at least once during pregnancy.

In 2017, based on screening conducted in selected family planning clinics in 10 funded jurisdictions, the proportion of patients who tested positive for gonorrhea was 26.5% for men who have sex with men (MSM), 14.6% for men who have sex with women, and 7.4% for women (https://www.cdc.gov/std/stats17/gonorrhea.htm).

Among those with HIV/AIDS, the prevalence of STIs is high; in one systematic review, the mean point prevalence of STIs was 16.3% in people living with HIV/AIDS. The most common STIs studied were syphilis (median 9.5% prevalence), gonorrhea (9.5%), chlamydia (5%), and trichomoniasis (18.8%).

In homeless populations, STI prevalence, including hepatitis C, ranges from 2.1% to 52.5% based on a systematic review; the reported prevalence of chlamydia/gonorrhea was highest among younger homeless adult women at 7.8%.

In a screening program for pharyngeal infection among MSM in San Francisco, out of a total of 12,454 pharyngeal chlamydia trachomatis (CT) specimens and 12,457 pharyngeal GC specimens, overall CT positivity was 1.69% (95% CI: 1.47-1.93) and GC positivity was 5.76% (95% CI: 5.36-6.19).

Authors of a systematic review of 115 reports found rectal prevalence of GC was 6.1% in MSM and 1.7% in women; prevalence of rectal CT was similar for MSM and women at 9% and 9.2%, respectively. These findings are supported by a second systematic review and meta-analysis reporting summary estimates of anorectal GC of 2.1% (95% CI 1.6 to 2.8) and anorectal CT of 8.0% (95% CI 7.0 to 9.1). Anal intercourse was a positive risk factor for GC (prevalence ratio 4.3, 95% CI 2.2 to 8.6) but not CT.

Total impact of all new sexually transmitted infections (STIs) is nearly $16 billion in direct medical costs in the United States (CDC, 2018); $1.1 billion are attributed to gonorrhea, chlamydia and syphilis.
Second most reported notifiable disease in the United States.
One in 5 people in the U.S. had an STI on any given day in 2018.

Anal gonorrhea is an independent risk factor for HIV acquisition. However, based on surveillance data collected at visits to sexual health clinics by MSM in England, rates of rectal gonorrhea increased from 3.5/100 person years to 11.1/100 person years between 2011 and 2018 while the rate of HIV incidence decreased by 22.3% for each percent increase in rectal gonorrhea.
STI caused by a Gram-negative diplococcus, N. gonorrhoeae.
Usually infects mucous membranes such as cervical mucosa, urethra, oral pharynx, or rectal area.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Prior or co-existing sexually transmitted infection
Rectal douching weekly or more prior to sex (MSM)

list.listitem: Assess all patients for STI behavioral risk factors and screen all sexually-active women aged 24 years and younger and older women at increased risk for gonorrhea. B
Screening is not recommended for low-risk men or women. A
Screen all pregnant patients at risk for gonorrhea (see Risk Factors) or living in an area in which the prevalence of N. gonorrhoeae is high at the first prenatal visit. A
The USPSTF (2020) recommends behavioral counseling for all sexually-active adolescents and for adults who are at increased risk for STIs. B

For MSM or transgender woman living with HIV or using preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) who are at high risk of STI (i.e., history of condomless anal or oral sex with a man and a diagnosis of gonorrhea, chlamydia, or early syphilis in the past 12 months), taking a single dose of doxycycline 200 mg within 24 hours to no more than 72 hours following condomless sexual intercourse reduces the risk of an STI. A Post-exposure prophylaxis has been less effective in other populations.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines note that primary prevention of STIs includes assessment of behavioral risk (i.e., assessing the sexual behaviors that can place persons at risk for infection) and biologic risk (i.e., testing for risk markers for STI and HIV acquisition or transmission). They suggest that healthcare providers routinely obtain sexual histories using the 5 P’s approach – sexual partners, practices, protection again STIs, past history of STIs, and pregnancy intention.
The USPSTF (2021) recommends screening all sexually-active women, including pregnant women, for gonorrhea infections if they are younger than 25 years or at high risk.
The USPSTF found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routine screening for gonorrhea infection in men at increased risk for infection.
USPSTF recommends against screening for gonorrhea in low-risk men or women.
USPSTF found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against screening all pregnant women for gonorrhea.

The CDC recommends screening for chlamydia and gonorrhea in the first trimester for pregnant patients less than 25 years of age and older pregnant patients at increased risk of infection (new or multiple sex partners, sex partner with concurrent partners, sex partners who have an STI). Screening for hepatitis B and C viruses, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis is recommended for all pregnant women. In the third trimester, screen for gonorrhea and hepatitis C for patients with ongoing risk and for chlamydia for patients less than 25 years of age and older pregnant patients at increased. HIV and syphilis screening is recommended in the third trimester for certain groups (see guidelines). Screen for STIs at delivery if not previously screened.

With respect to screening MSM, authors of a systematic review of 12 studies found little evidence that screening for GC or CT influenced the prevalence of these infections. In an RCT from Belgium including 1014 MSM and transgender women taking PrEP comparing screening with non-screening for N gonorrhoeae and C trachomatis, screening was associated with higher antibiotic consumption but had no effect on the incidence of N gonorrhoeae.

Routine screening may not be warranted in refugee populations. Authors of one study of 18,516 individuals who received STI testing as part of screening medical examinations in Minnesota during 2003 to 2010 found low rates of STIs (1.1% were seropositive for syphilis, 0.6% were positive for chlamydia, and 0.2% were positive for gonorrhea).

Similarly, low detection rates were found in a study of infertile Canadian men (0.304% positive for chlamydia and 0.0537% positive for gonorrhea), making routine screening of little value in this population.

listitem.strong: Strategies that increase STI screening rates

list.listitem: Strategies that increase STI screening rates among MSM include regular serological screening for syphilis during routine HIV care, syphilis serology included with blood tests performed as part of HIV monitoring, use of an electronic medical record computer alert, and an electronic medical record system to enhance syphilis retesting after syphilis treatment.
Home-based screening significantly increases uptake and was the preferred screening strategy in 3/6 trials.
The USPSTF (2020) recommends behavioral counseling for all sexually-active adolescents and for adults who are at increased risk for STIs.

A 15-minute interactive computerized video was effective in increasing condom use and decreasing new cases of STIs (gonorrhea and chlamydia incidence 6% in the intervention group vs 13% in the control group). Similar benefit was seen in an RCT of counseling and recontact at an STI clinic.
Patient-centered risk-reduction counseling at the time of rapid HIV testing did not reduce subsequent acquisition of STIs.
Periodic presumptive treatment is effective in reducing prevalence of gonorrhoea, chlamydia, and ulcerative STIs among sex workers, based on results of a systematic review.

In an RCT including 501 MSM and transgender women who were either living with HIV (n = 174) or using PrEP (n = 327), both intervention groups randomized to taking a single dose of doxycycline 200 mg within 24 hours to no more than 72 hours following condomless sexual intercourse compared to controls had lower rates of an STI at a median of 9-months follow-up (11.8% vs 30.5%; NNT = 5 and 10.7% vs 31.9%; NNT = 5, respectively).

Among cisgender women in Kenya, the incidence of STIs was not significantly lower with doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis following condomless sex compared to standard care in an open-label trial including 449 women aged 18-30 years. There were 109 incident STIs of which chlamydia accounted for 78%. Relative risk of incident STI over 12 months was 0.88 (95% CI 0.6 to 1.3). Among 50 randomly selected participants in the doxycycline group, doxycycline was detected in 29% of hair samples. All N. gonorrhoeae-positive isolates were resistant to doxycycline.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 studies found doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis was associated with an increased prevalence of tetracycline resistance in N. gonorrhoeae which did not reach statistical significance (pooled OR 2.3, 95% CI 0.9-3.4).
There is good evidence that nonoxynol-9 does not protect against STIs, including gonorrhea (RR 0.91; 95% CI: 0.67-1.24).
Similarly, use of hormonal contraception does not protect against GC.

There is some effectiveness of meningococcal B outer membrane vesicle vaccines against gonorrhea incidence, with reported adjusted vaccine effectiveness ranging from 22% to 46% and pooled effectiveness estimates following the full vaccine series of 33-34% based on a meta-analysis of 12 studies primarily targeting individuals aged 15-30 years.
Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) have high specificities and sensitivities and can be used on urethral, endocervical, or urine samples. A
Point-of-care testing should be reserved for those patients for whom follow-up care is unlikely, although test characteristics continue to improve. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Difficult to distinguish between the 2 infections
Difficult to distinguish between the 2 infections

list.listitem: Men develop symptoms 1 to 14 days after exposure; many men are asymptomatic.
Symptoms include penile discharge, dysuria, or urethral pruritus.
Occasionally the infection will ascend to the epididymis and cause testicular and/or scrotal pain and discomfort.
Mucopurulent discharge from the penis may be present; if not, milking the shaft of the penis may produce the discharge.
Women tend to be asymptomatic with gonococcal cervicitis.
If women have symptoms, they report mucopurulent vaginal discharge, dysuria and/or vaginal bleeding between periods.
Lower genital tract infections in women can ascend to the upper genital tract and cause pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).
Rectal symptoms in men and women include discharge, anal itching, soreness, bleeding, or painful bowel movements.
Physical examination will show mucopurulent discharge from the endocervical canal.
If PID is present, cervical motion tenderness and/or adnexal mass can be present.

Rarely gonococcal infections can become disseminated, with polyarticular tenosynovitis and dermatitis. In a single institution case series of 112 women hospitalized with disseminated gonococcal infection, with one exception, all had arthritis involving a mean of two joints, most commonly the knee and wrist.
A prospective study of 288 women found that adding pelvic examination to the history does not improve diagnostic accuracy.

Gram stain of men's first-voided urine; if more than 5 WBCs per oil immersion is present, consider this a positive test for urethritis. If negative, does not rule out gonococcal infection. In one study in men, gram stain with 5 or more WBC had a sensitivity, specificity and positive likelihood ratio of 26% (95% CI: 18-33), 91% (95% CI: 87-94) and 2.7 (95% CI: 1.8-4.2), respectively, for the diagnosis of culture positive urethritis. The sensitivity of Gram stain to N. gonorrhoeae was highest among the infections at 80% (95% CI: 64-96).
Positive leukocyte esterase or more than 10 WBCs/high powered field (HPF) suggests an infectious cause of urethritis in men.

In one review, nine studies of leucocyte esterase dipstick testing had a median sensitivity of 71% (range 23%-85%), median specificity of 70% (33%-99%), median positive predictive value (PPV) of 19% (5%-40%) and median negative predictive value (NPV) of 95% (56%-99%); a median of three steps were involved in testing and took under 2 minutes. In three studies of immunochromatographic strips, median sensitivity was 70% (60%-94%), median specificity was 96% (89%-97%), median PPV was 56% (55%-97%) and median NPV was 93% (92%-99%); these test strips involved five to seven steps and took 15 to 30 minutes to complete.

In an Australian study of the benefit of microscopy in 150 gay or bisexual men with proctitis, microscopy did not reliably provide information necessary to tailor management. Discharge found on proctoscopy, positive HIV status, and time since last receptive anal intercourse were independent predictors of NAAT positivity for any rectal STI.
NAAT has largely replaced culture techniques for testing for gonococcal infections. The tests have good sensitivity (92%-96%) and specificity (94%-99%) and are recommended by the CDC (2021).

NAAT can be performed on endocervical, vaginal, urethral (men), or urine samples (both men and women) with similar sensitivity and specificity. Authors of a systematic review of 9 publications found that vaginal specimens had similar NAAT performance to cervical and urine specimens for GC (performance estimates: vaginal 64%-100%, cervical 85%-100%, urine 67%-94%) and CT (performance estimates: vaginal 65%-100%, cervical 59%-97%, urine 57%-100%). In a more recent meta-analysis, overall sensitivity for detecting chlamydia, gonorrhea, or trichomonas in women was greater with vaginal samples than urine samples. Vaginal sampling was more acceptable to women and of lower cost.

As male urethral swabs are painful, urine testing should be the preferred testing method; if direct sampling is desired, a plastic loop appears to be less painful than a rayon or Dacron swab. A study of 634 men, however, found self-obtained penile-meatal swabs resulted in detection of more chlamydia, gonorrhea, and trichomonas than urine specimens.
The CDC cautions providers to read the product inserts for each NAAT manufacturer because collection methods and specimen types vary.
Culture is available for detection of rectal, oropharyngeal, and conjunctival gonococcal infection, as NAAT is not FDA-cleared for use with these specimens.

A NAAT assay, Bio-Rad Dx CT/NG/MG appears to be both highly sensitive and specific for the simultaneous detection of C. trachomatis, M. genitalium and N. gonorrhoeae in urogenital specimens of symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals.

Pooling samples after swabbing from different anatomical sites (pharynx, vagina, rectum) for NAAT demonstrates similar results compared to separate testing, with slight decreased sensitivity. In a study of 489 patients tested, from whom 42 tested positive on at least one non-pooled sample, only 5 gave a negative result on the pooled sample (sensitivity 82% [95% CI 57% to 96%] for NG and 94% [95% CI 79% to 99% for chlamydia].

In cases of child sexual assault involving boys, rectal and oropharyngeal infections in prepubescent girls, and evaluation of potential treatment failure, culture and susceptibility testing may be required.
Optimal recovery rates of N. gonorrhoeae are achieved when specimens are inoculated directly and when the growth medium is promptly incubated in an increased CO2 environment.

A self-collected sample (rectal, pharyngeal, or vaginal swab) is a feasible, valid, and acceptable alternative to provider-collected sampling. When an STI is suspected, both specificity and sensitivity of a patient administered vaginal PCR swab are high for detecting chlamydia or gonorrhea (LR+ 91 and LR− 0.09). In a large cohort study from a single STI clinic of 3859 women tested for gonorrhea, vaginal self-swabbing was as sensitive and specific as endocervical and vaginal nucleic acid assay and more sensitive than culture.
In a study of MSM, self-administered testing was significantly better at identifying pharyngeal and rectal gonorrhea than clinician testing; chlamydia detection rates were similar.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 45 primarily observational studies found high self-sampling pooled specificity for both genital and extragenital testing (>99.0%, 95% CI 98.2%-99.5%) but variable sensitivity with differences noted between vaginal (79.6%, 95% CI 62.1%-90.3%) and extragenital testing (>91.6%, 95% CI 86.0%-95.1%). Self-sampling was highly acceptable (80.0%-100.0%; n=24), reached 51%-70% (n=3) of first-time testers and resulted in 89%-100% (n=3) linkages to care.

Testing at home was evaluated in 19 studies, including 15 RCTs with 62,369 participants and four concordance studies with 906 participants. Authors of this meta-analysis found higher uptake (OR 2.61) with at home testing compared with clinical settings and there was high concordance between specimens collected in both settings and no significant difference in linkage to care

Samples from SurePath liquid-based Pap can also be tested for chlamydia and gonorrhea; in one case series with 394 women of whom C. trachomatis was present in 8.9%, and N. gonorrhoeae in 1.5%, all testing assays showed high specificity although sensitivity was highest for chlamydia on Aptima Combo 2 assay. In another study of 1838 subjects, SurePath using the GCQ assay had sensitivity and specificity of 95.3% and 99.95%, respectively.

The rapid Cepheid GeneXpert CT/NG (Xpert) assay demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity compared with NAAT for endocervical, vaginal, and urine samples from women and urine samples from men. In contrast, sensitivity for gonorrhea with ACON Duo compared to NAAT was only 12.5% and specificity 99.8%.

Point-of-care testing is available but is often less sensitive and less specific than NAATs sent to reference laboratories. To date, point-of-care testing should be reserved for cases in which follow-up is judged as unlikely to occur.

Authors of a literature review of rapid tests found that the best point-of-care test for gonorrhea, GC Check, had a sensitivity of 54% to 70% and specificity of 97% to 98%. This translates into 14 to 18 additional patients treated at first attendance, 28 to 32 undiagnosed, and 92 to 137 false-positives for every 100 patients diagnosed. In contrast, the best rapid NAAT for gonorrhea, GeneXpert, had a sensitivity of 96% to 100% and specificity of 99.9% to 100% resulting in no additional patients being treated at first attendance, 0 to 4 undiagnosed, and 0 to 5 false-positives. Rapid NAAT also reduced time to initiation of treatment by 4 days.

In a study conducted in an ED of 1162 urine samples, investigators found excellent kappa agreement between the rapid Xpert CT/NG Assay (Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA) and a traditional assay (Aptima Combo 2): NG for men, 1.00; 95% CI: 1.00-1.00 and NG for women, 0.87; 95% CI: 0.79-0.94. Agreement was somewhat less for CT detection (men, 0.81; 95% CI: 0.59-1.00 and women: 0.85; 95% CI: 0.80-0.90).

In a study conducted in remote primary healthcare settings of diagnostic performance of point-of-care GeneXpert CT/NG run in parallel on 2486 self-collected urine or vaginal specimens with conventional laboratory-based NAATs, NG concordance was 99.9% (95% CI: 99.7 to 100.0) with a positive concordance of 100.0% (95% CI: 97.5 to 100.0) and negative concordance of 99.9% (95% CI: 99.7 to 100.0). CT concordance was also high at 99.4% (95% CI: 99.1 to 99.7).
Obtain a sexual history to determine STI behavioral risk factors and screen all women aged 24 years and younger and older women at increased risk for gonorrhea.

Physical findings in women include mucopurulent discharge from the endocervical canal. Men usually have symptoms of dysuria when they have gonococcal urethritis. There may be a mucopurulent penile discharge present. If not visible, milking the shaft of the penis can be performed.

Multiple anatomic sites for testing should be considered. In an STI clinic study of 2436 men and 1321 women on whom anorectal, oropharyngeal and urogenital samples were obtained, gonorrhea was identified in 6.3% of men and 3.1% of women. Isolated non-urogenital infections accounted for 76% of all infections in men and about half of all infections in women.
Specimens can be successfully self-collected.
If infection is suspected, NAAT is FDA-approved for performance on endocervical, vaginal, urethral, or urine samples.
Testing for women of the endocervical canal should include chlamydia because of high rate of dual infections.
Testing in men can be done by using NAAT on urine.

CDC recommends performing culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing in cases of suspected or documented treatment failure, because non-culture tests can’t provide antimicrobial susceptibility results.
Empiric treatment of both men and women should be performed if the risk of gonorrhea infection is high.

The CDC recommends that recent sex partners, defined as persons having sexual contact with the infected patient within the 60 days preceding onset of symptoms or gonorrhea diagnosis or the most recent sex partner if more than 60 days, be referred for evaluation, testing, and presumptive dual treatment. To avoid reinfection, sex partners should be instructed to abstain from unprotected sexual intercourse for 7 days after they and their sexual partner(s) have completed treatment and after resolution of symptoms, if present.

Expedited partner therapy (the clinical practice of treating the sex partners of patients diagnosed with chlamydia or gonorrhea by providing prescriptions or medications to the patient to take to his/her partner without the health care provider first examining the partner) should be strongly considered.
Samples from MSM appear to be significantly more likely to exhibit antimicrobial-resistant N. gonorrhoeae with elevated MICs of ceftriaxone and azithromycin than for men who have sex with women.

Treat gonococcal infection of the cervix, urethra, pharynx and/or rectum with ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly (IM) as a single dose. Patients weighing more than 300 pounds should be given a dose of 1 gram. (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC, 2020). A
If chlamydia infection has not been excluded, add doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days or if pregnant a single dose of azithromycin 1 gram orally. A

Recent sex partners (i.e., persons having sexual contact with the infected patient <60 days preceding onset of symptoms or gonorrhea diagnosis) should be referred for evaluation, testing, and presumptive treatment. If referral is not possible, expedited partner treatment can be delivered to the partner by the patient or a collaborating pharmacy as permitted by law.

Based on increasing concern for antimicrobial stewardship, the continued low incidence of ceftriaxone resistance, and the increased incidence of azithromycin resistance, the CDC recommends ceftriaxone 500 mg IM to treat gonococcal infection of the cervix, urethra, pharynx and/or rectum. Patients weighing more than 300 pounds should be given a dose of 1 gram. If chlamydia infection has not been excluded, add doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days or if pregnant single dose of azithromycin 1 gram orally.(Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC, 2020).
Gonococcal conjunctivitis in adults is treated with ceftriaxone 1 g plus azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose

If ceftriaxone is not available or in the event of cephalosporin allergy, the recommended alternative regimen is gentamicin 240 mg IM as a single dose plus azithromycin 2 grams orally as a single dose or cefixime 800 mg orally as a single dose. As with ceftriaxone, if chlamydia has not been excluded treat for chlamydia with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, and if pregnant, with azithromycin 1 gram orally as a single dose.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs found a pooled efficacy of cefixime of 97% with no significant difference with comparison drugs; risk of bias, however, was high.

In an RCT including 161 patients with uncomplicated urogenital, rectal, or pharyngeal gonorrhea conducted in the Czech Republic, single dose ceftriaxone 1 g intramuscularly plus single dose oral azithromycin 2 g was similarly effective to oral cefixime 800 mg plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for negative culture at 1 week (100% in both), but more effective with respect to negative culture at 3 weeks (100% vs. 92%) and for NAAT at 3 weeks after treatment initiation (100% vs. 87%). All treatment failures observed in the cefixime arm were pharyngeal gonorrhea cases.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 20 studies confirmed that 800 mg single dose cefixime was highly effective at treating urogenital infections (98%, 95% CI, 96%-99%) but less effective for treating pharyngeal infections (81%, 95% CI 61%-92%).
Global prevalence of N. gonorrhoeae resistance rates over the past 30 years were 6% for azithromycin and 48% for erythromycin.

Rates of resistance to gonorrhea to ceftriaxone remain low. The CDC reports that elevated ceftriaxone minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), defined as ≥0.125 µg/ml, fluctuated between 0.05% and 0.4%, elevated cefixime MICs of ≥0.25 µg/ml declined from 1.4% in 2011 to 0.4% in 2017, and elevated azithromycin MICs of ≥2 µg/ml increased during 2014–2017 from 2.5% to 4.4%.
Fluoroquinolones are not acceptable alternatives because of the increased resistance. For the same reason, azithromycin is only recommended in pregnancy when doxycycline is contraindicated.
Gentamycin 40 mg IM as a single dose plus azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose can also be used when ceftriaxone is unavailable.

In an RCT in England, however, comparing 1 g oral azithromycin PLUS a single IM injection of 500 mg ceftriaxone OR 240 mg gentamicin for treatment of uncomplicated gonorrhea, patients randomized to ceftriaxone had higher rates of negative follow-up tests vs. gentamicin (98% vs. 91%, respectively), especially for those with pharyngeal gonorrhea (96% vs. 80%, respectively). Rates of adverse effects were comparable. It might be considered in cases of cephalosporin unavailability or allergy.

In an RCT comparing zoliflodacin 2 grams orally single dose, zoliflodacin 3 grams orally single dose, or ceftriaxone 500 mg IMI single dose in patients with urogenital gonorrhea, urogenital cure was confirmed in 96% receiving zoliflodacin 2 grams, 96% receiving the 3-gram dose, and 100% in those receiving ceftriaxone. The drug was somewhat less effective at curing pharyngeal infections, and non-serious GI adverse effects were relatively common, especially with the 3-gram dose.

In a 4-arm RCT including 346 patients with anogenital gonorrhea randomized to ceftriaxone (n=103), ertapenem (n=103), gentamicin (n=102), or fosfomycin (n=38), single-dose 1000 mg ertapenem was non-inferior to single-dose 500 mg ceftriaxone for clearance of gonorrhea. Gentamicin was less effective at 5 mg/kg gentamicin (maximum 400 mg) to ceftriaxone and treatment with fosfomycin treatment was terminated early due to poor efficacy.

A recent industry-sponsored RCT conducted at 49 centers in multiple countries found that oral gepotidacin, approved by the FDA in March 2025, had efficacy comparable to that of intramuscular ceftriaxone plus oral azithromycin for the treatment of uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhea. However, gepotidacin was associated with more adverse effects and is considerably more expensive than standard therapy.
Recommendation in nonpregnant women and men is to rescreen at 3 months after the initial infection.

For patients treated with an alternative regimen, a test-of-cure is recommended 14 days after treatment using either culture or NAAT. If the NAAT is positive, perform a confirmatory culture before retreatment.
Pregnant patients should be tested for a cure 3 weeks after treatment because of the potential negative impact on a newborn.
Untreated gonorrhea in men can cause an ascending infection in the epididymis.
Untreated gonorrhea in women can cause tubular-factor infertility, PID and rarely pericapsular hepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome).

A significant proportion of asymptomatic patients appear to clear gonorrhea infections spontaneously. In a secondary analysis of an RCT of treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea, spontaneous clearance (defined as a positive pre-enrollment NAAT result followed by a negative NAAT at enrollment) occurred in 32 of 221 (14.5%) patients with anal, 17 of 91 (18.7%) with pharyngeal, 3 of 13 (23.1%) with vaginal and 9 of 28 (32.1%) with urethral gonorrhea infections.
Treatment provides a high percentage of cure.

The cure rate for urogenital gonorrhea is high, but the reinfection rate is also high. Because of this, the current recommendation in nonpregnant women and men is to rescreen them at 3 months after the initial infection.

The STI 2021 guidelines recommend a test of cure at 7-14 days after initial treatment for any person with pharyngeal gonorrhea using either culture or NAAT. Testing at 7 days might result in an increased likelihood of a false-positive test.
Text message reminders to return for retesting were not effective in one RCT.

In contrast, authors of a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs found active recall significantly improved reattendance/retesting rates (pooled OR 2.42; 95% CI: 1.84-3.19). Home sampling also increased retesting compared with clinic testing.

Pregnant patients should be tested for a cure 3 weeks after treatment because of the potential negative impact of gonorrhea on a newborn including eye, skin, respiratory and systemic infection with meningitis.
Avoid sexual contact for at least 7 days after completion of therapy.

Recent sex partners (i.e., persons having sexual contact with the infected patient <60 days preceding onset of symptoms or gonorrhea diagnosis) should be referred for evaluation, testing, and presumptive treatment.

Partner notification and offering treatment have been shown to have a positive influence on recurrence rates. Authors of a Cochrane review were not able to find an optimal strategy for partner notification.

If referral is not possible, expedited partner treatment can be delivered to the partner by the patient or a collaborating pharmacy as permitted by law. Expedited partner therapy is superior to standard partner referral for treatment and for reducing rates of re-infection.
Screening for HIV should be offered to all patients who have an STI.
Condom use has been shown to reduce the risk for gonorrhea infections.

Worldwide pooled prevalence of gonorrhea in pregnant women was estimated at 1.85% (95% CI 1.73-1.97%). The highest rate was in the African region (3.53%, 95% CI 2.84-4.29%) and lowest rate in the European region (0.52%, 95% CI 0.27-0.84%).

In a large database study of 354,217 pregnant women of whom 0.6% had a gonorrhea notification, women with gonorrhea had an increased risk for preterm birth (aOR 2.50; 95% CI: 1.39-4.50) and stillbirth (aOR 2.35; 95% CI: 0.58-9.56).

In an RCT including 4526 pregnant patients in Papua New Guinea, point-of-care testing and treatment of chlamydia, gonorrhea, T. vaginalis, and bacterial vaginosis did not reduce preterm birth and/or low birthweight compared with standard care (18.8% vs.17.8%). However, within the subgroup of women with gonorrhea, there was a substantial reduction in the primary outcome.

Treatment options for pregnant and nonpregnant women are the same as above; however, high-quality trials in pregnant women are lacking. Azithromycin 1 g single dose is also recommended if chlamydia infection has not been excluded.

During 2010 to 2015, 3703 CT/GC conjunctivitis cases were reported to CDC from the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia. Rates of GC conjunctivitis remained stable at 0.2 cases or less per 100,000 live births annually.

The USPSTF (2019) recommends prophylactic ocular topical medication for all newborns to prevent gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum. (A recommendation). The CDC recommends erythromycin (0.5%) ophthalmic ointment in each eye in a single application at birth.

In a retrospective study of charts of 1319 children ages 0 to 17 years who were consecutively evaluated for sexual victimization, CT was identified in 104 patients and GC in 33. Despite most children not reporting rectal or oral contact with the assailant's genitals, 51 patients had positive anal tests and 24 had positive oral tests.

N. gonorrhoeae infection in prepubertal children is not always because of sexual transmission; communal baths, towels or fabric, rectal thermometers, and caregivers hands are also potential means of transmission.

Neonatal conjunctivitis is treated with ceftriaxone 25 to 50 mg/kg IV or IM in a single dose not to exceed 125 mg; infants born to mothers with untreated gonococcal infections should be similarly treated.
Children more than 45 kg with gonococcal infection are treated similarly to adults.
Children 45 kg or less with uncomplicated gonococcal infection are treated with ceftriaxone 25 to 50 mg/kg IV or IM in a single dose not to exceed 125 mg.
